Jews do not typically turn over individuals to Roman authorities for blasphemy; they would stone such a person instead. So, we know that Romans killed Jesus, likely due to his threat to their social structure. However, the Bible states that it was the Jews who killed Jesus.

Pilate, a Roman governor, took custody of Jesus and had him flogged. He then put a crown of thorns on Jesus' head and dressed him in a purple robe, mocking him by saying "Hail, king of the Jews" and striking him. Pilate went out to them again and said, "I can find no case against this man." He brought Jesus outside, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, and told them, "Here is the man." The chief priests and police shouted for his crucifixion.

The Bible claims that Jews killed Jesus, which suggests the text may not be entirely reliable. This leads us to Paul's story. At this time, Paul was persecuting Christians as a Pharisee on the road to Damascus when he had a light-seized vision of Jesus telling him to stop persecuting. This conversion makes no sense as a story but is what Christians believe.

Saul, still threatening and murdering Christians, went to the high priest for letters to arrest more followers. He arrived in Damascus with these letters, intending to find and bind any Christians he could. As he approached Damascus, a light flashed around him, and he fell to the ground, hearing a voice asking, "Why do you persecute me?" Saul asked who it was, and heard the reply, "I am Jesus. Get up and enter the city; you will be told what to do." His companions saw the light but did not see anyone. Saul got up, could not see for three days, and neither ate nor drank.

This narrative highlights a significant conversion and a miracle that parallels Plato's allegory of the cave, reflecting Paul’s background in Greek culture.
